title: MedSync clerking diagnosis reasoning catalogue
scope: Adult (15 and over) internal-medicine outpatient, emergency and ward clerking at a Ugandan referral hospital. The reasoning layer for step 09 Impression: what supports or argues against each diagnosis, what has not been asked or examined, which tests would help decide, must-not-miss marking, and differential suggestions. Paediatric, obstetric and surgical-specialty reasoning are later rounds.

owners.terminology: REF-DX-TERMS (data/emr/diagnosis-terms.v1.json): display, synonyms, chronic flag, sensitivity, ICD-11. Never copied here.
owners.tests: medsync.test-catalogue (data/emr/test-catalogue.v1.json): orderable tests. This file only names test ids.
owners.history_ids: MS-EMR-CLERK-CAT-001 (sym.*, red flags, past, family, medicines, social, REF-FLAG-*).

conventions.ids: Profiles are keyed by the REF-DX-TERMS id (dx.*). Rules are DDX-*; references REF-DX-*; tests test.*. The app stores ids, never labels.
conventions.evidence: suggest_for and suggest_against are atoms in the shared rule language (flag_rule_language of the history and examination catalogues, plus family_condition, medicine, social and news2_total). When an atom is true for this encounter the evidence matrix shows a SUGGESTED mark (dotted outline, "Suggested") in that cell. A suggestion is never stored, never counted and never written to the note until the clinician accepts it (one tap on the cell or "Accept suggested" per column). Unrecorded is never evidence against anything.
conventions.ask: ask lists history questions and examination items that would help weigh this diagnosis. If the target is unanswered for this encounter it appears under "Not asked yet" (history) or "Not examined yet" (examination). Answering writes to the owner of that fact (the history or examination step), never to this catalogue or a private copy.
conventions.tests: tests_to_decide lists test ids; "Add to plan" creates a draft order through the plan step. Nothing is ordered on suggestion alone.
conventions.must_not_miss: A must-not-miss diagnosis on the differential stays pinned above the others until the clinician marks it Unlikely with a written reason; the reason is stored and written to the note. Must-not-miss is a property of the diagnosis, not of the patient: it never raises a flag by itself.
conventions.time_critical: time_critical marks diagnoses where delay harms within hours. The row shows "Time-critical" with a clock icon; the Flags panel is not changed by this catalogue.
conventions.severity: none, clinician (the clinician picks from options; nothing is graded automatically), classifier (the named examination classifier result is shown and may be accepted as the grade), or named_scale (a published scale the clinician applies; options listed). An unsigned scale shows "Awaiting sign-off".
conventions.onset: Allowed onsets for the diagnosis and the default offered. Chronic diagnoses can be offered to the problem list.
conventions.problem_list: offer (offer "Add to problem list" when working or final), offer_when_final, never.
conventions.restricted: restricted_class mirrors D-CFC-09 (hiv, tb, mental_health, sexual_reproductive_health). Restricted profiles, their suggestions and their evidence rows are shown only to clinicians with access and never appear in patient-facing text. A restricted diagnosis is never suggested to a viewer without access.
conventions.suggestions: ddx_rules suggest diagnoses to consider from the history and examination. They are decision support: shown under "Also considered with these findings" with their reason, added only by the clinician, never ranked, never marked likely, never written to the note unless added.
conventions.statuses: draft, draft-verified-source, draft-unverified, signed. A rule or reference that is not signed does not fire.
conventions.language: en-GB. Findings, not interpretations. No doses anywhere in this file.

kinds.exposure: An exposure that needs action before disease (rabies exposure).

REF-DX-HYPOTHERMIA-TEMP.meaning: Below this temperature, hypothermia is suggested as supporting evidence (core temperature confirms).

REF-DX-HYPOTHERMIA-STAGES.meaning: Stage bands shown beside the clinician-graded hypothermia stage (never applied automatically).

REF-DX-HYPERPYREXIA.meaning: At or above this, heat stroke and severe infection are suggested for consideration.

REF-DX-HR-RAISED.meaning: At or above this pulse, "tachycardia" counts as suggested evidence (NEWS2 scoring band starts here).

REF-DX-HR-FAST.meaning: At or above this pulse, arrhythmia and shock are suggested (NEWS2 scores 3).

REF-DX-BRADY.meaning: Below this pulse, "bradycardia" counts as suggested evidence.

REF-DX-HR-VERY-LOW.meaning: Below this pulse, heart block and severe hypothermia are suggested (NEWS2 scores 3 at 40 or less).

REF-DX-RR-RAISED.meaning: At or above this respiratory rate, tachypnoea counts as suggested evidence (NEWS2 scores 2 from 21).

REF-DX-RR-LOW.meaning: Below this respiratory rate, opioid or sedative toxicity and raised intracranial pressure are suggested (NEWS2 scores 3 at 8 or less).

REF-DX-SPO2-LOW.meaning: Below this SpO2 on scale 1, hypoxaemia counts as suggested evidence (NEWS2 scores 3 at 91 or less).

REF-DX-BP-HTN.meaning: Clinic BP at or above either value counts as suggested evidence of hypertension (a diagnosis needs repeat readings).

REF-DX-BP-OBST-SEVERE.meaning: In pregnancy or up to 6 weeks postpartum, BP at or above either value is severe hypertension (severe pre-eclampsia range).

REF-DX-GLU-HHS.meaning: At or above this glucose, HHS is weighted over DKA (with high osmolality and little ketosis; results needed to confirm).

REF-DX-SBP-VERY-HIGH.meaning: At or above this systolic, intracerebral haemorrhage is weighted in stroke (clinician weighs; never decides).

REF-DX-GLU-RANDOM-DM.meaning: Random plasma glucose at or above this value WITH symptoms is in the diabetes range (WHO: 'to be used only in the presence of symptoms')

dx.aaa_rupture.must_not_miss_reason: A ruptured aortic aneurysm is fatal within hours without surgery and is often misdiagnosed as renal colic or back strain.
dx.aaa_rupture.note: Uncommon in sub-Saharan populations, so easily forgotten; consider it in an older male smoker with collapse and abdominal, back or loin pain. A bedside ultrasound of the aorta decides fastest.

dx.abdominal_pain_unexplained.note: Pregnancy test in every woman of reproductive age before imaging or labelling. Medical causes that present as abdominal pain include DKA, sickle cell crisis, malaria, pyelonephritis and inferior myocardial infarction.

dx.acs.must_not_miss_reason: Missed myocardial infarction or unstable angina carries high early mortality, and the benefit of reperfusion and antithrombotic treatment falls with every hour.
dx.acs.note: A 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes; a normal first ECG or troponin does not exclude it, and women, older people and people with diabetes often present with breathlessness or epigastric pain. Incidence is rising in Uganda; check both-arm BP before antithrombotics.

dx.acute_bronchitis.note: A diagnosis of exclusion: tachypnoea, hypoxaemia, focal chest signs or confusion mean pneumonia, and cough for two weeks or more (any duration with HIV) means TB screening. Most cases are viral and self-limiting.

dx.acute_limb_ischaemia.must_not_miss_reason: Muscle and nerve die within about six hours of complete arterial occlusion; revascularisation must not wait.
dx.acute_limb_ischaemia.note: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, cold, paraesthesia and paralysis; any sensory loss or weakness means an immediately threatened limb. In Uganda the usual source is embolism from rheumatic AF or a dilated heart; there is no limb-pulse item or arterial imaging test in the catalogues yet.

dx.acute_liver_failure.must_not_miss_reason: Cerebral oedema, bleeding, hypoglycaemia and sepsis kill within days; paracetamol and some other causes have specific time-dependent treatment.
dx.acute_liver_failure.note: Jaundice with encephalopathy and INR 1.5 or more within 26 weeks and no prior cirrhosis; in Uganda think HBV, hepatitis E (severe in pregnancy), anti-TB drugs, herbal remedies and paracetamol. Severe malaria, leptospirosis, yellow fever and VHF mimic it; chronic liver stigmata are not used against it, because gynaecomastia and palmar erythema are non-specific (efavirenz, spironolactone) and acute-on-chronic failure is as lethal.

dx.adrenal_insufficiency.must_not_miss_reason: Adrenal crisis (shock, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia) is fatal within hours yet cheap and quick to treat.
dx.adrenal_insufficiency.note: In sub-Saharan Africa adrenal TB and HIV-related disease are the main causes; rifampicin and stopping long-term steroids (including steroid-containing herbal preparations) can unmask it. Hyperpigmentation is hard to read in dark skin and has no examination item, and steroid use has no medicine answer yet.

dx.af.note: In young Ugandans AF usually means rheumatic mitral disease, which changes stroke prevention: echo every new AF. Seek a precipitant: thyrotoxicosis, sepsis, alcohol, PE.

dx.aki.note: Check potassium first: hyperkalaemia is what kills within hours. In Uganda sepsis, severe malaria, dehydration, herbal remedies and NSAIDs dominate; exclude obstruction with a bladder scan or ultrasound.

dx.alcohol_dependence.note: Uganda has among the highest per-capita alcohol use in Africa, much of it local spirits (waragi) or brews; AUDIT is not yet in the catalogue. Self-reported use under-reads, so a recorded "none" argues only weakly against; screen for liver disease, depression and self-harm.

dx.alcohol_intoxication.note: Never attribute reduced consciousness to alcohol until glucose, head injury and co-ingestion are addressed. Visual blurring with deep breathing after local spirits suggests methanol, which has caused outbreaks in Uganda.

dx.alcohol_withdrawal.must_not_miss_reason: Untreated withdrawal can progress to seizures and delirium tremens, which carry significant mortality, and Wernicke encephalopathy may coexist.
dx.alcohol_withdrawal.note: Onset is typically 6 to 24 hours after the last drink, with delirium tremens at 48 to 72 hours. Fever or disorientation need a search for infection, subdural haematoma and hypoglycaemia before being attributed to withdrawal.

dx.alcoholic_hepatitis.note: Needs heavy drinking up to weeks before onset; AST is usually under 300 IU/L and above ALT, which helps separate it from viral or drug hepatitis. Self-reported alcohol use under-reads, infection and HBV co-infection mimic and complicate it, and the severity grade (Maddrey or similar) has no source id yet.

dx.anaemia_unexplained.note: Anaemia is very common in adult medical admissions; malaria, hookworm, HIV (and zidovudine), GI and menstrual blood loss and sickle cell are the common causes. MCV and reticulocytes split loss, deficiency, haemolysis and marrow failure.

dx.anaphylaxis.must_not_miss_reason: Airway obstruction, bronchospasm and circulatory collapse can kill within minutes; immediate adrenaline is the treatment.
dx.anaphylaxis.note: A clinical diagnosis: treatment must never wait for a test, and mast cell tryptase is not in the test catalogue. There is no allergen-exposure question (food, drug, sting, contrast); ask it in free text, and remember skin signs are absent in a minority.

dx.angina_stable.note: Separating stable angina from ACS needs relief within minutes of rest and a pattern stable over weeks, which the history catalogue does not yet capture. Exclude aortic stenosis and severe anaemia, both common causes of exertional chest pain here.

dx.angioedema.must_not_miss_reason: Tongue, floor-of-mouth and laryngeal swelling can obstruct the airway within minutes to hours.
dx.angioedema.note: ACE-inhibitor angioedema has no urticaria or itch, can start years into treatment and responds poorly to adrenaline; enalapril is the only ACE inhibitor on the medicine list. Chronic periorbital puffiness from nephrotic syndrome or pre-eclampsia is not angioedema (archive, oedema).

dx.anxiety_disorder.note: Exclude thyrotoxicosis, arrhythmia, hypoglycaemia, asthma, alcohol withdrawal and khat or caffeine use before labelling. Anxiety and depression often coexist.

dx.aortic_dissection.must_not_miss_reason: Untreated type A dissection has a high hourly mortality, and treating it as ACS with antithrombotics or thrombolysis can be fatal.

suggest_for.text: BP difference between arms above REF-EX-ARM-DIFF

dx.aortic_dissection.note: Tearing pain maximal at onset and radiating to the back is the classic history; the history catalogue does not yet capture pain character or radiation. Check BP in both arms before any antithrombotic for presumed ACS.

dx.aortic_stenosis.note: In Uganda rheumatic aortic disease presents decades earlier than calcific stenosis, often with mitral disease. Exertional syncope, angina or breathlessness mark severe stenosis with a risk of sudden death; echo decides.

dx.appendicitis.must_not_miss_reason: Perforation and peritonitis follow delay, and in women a ruptured ectopic pregnancy presents the same way.
dx.appendicitis.note: A pregnancy test is mandatory in any woman of reproductive age with right iliac fossa pain. Ileocaecal TB, typhoid and mesenteric adenitis are local mimics; migration of pain to the right iliac fossa has no history item yet.

dx.ascites_unexplained.note: The ascitic tap (albumin gradient, cells, culture) splits portal hypertension from peritoneal causes. TB peritonitis, hepatitis B cirrhosis, hepatosplenic schistosomiasis and endomyocardial fibrosis are important Ugandan causes.

dx.aspiration_pneumonia.note: Follows reduced consciousness, seizures, alcohol or dysphagia; poisoning, including organophosphates, is a common cause in Uganda. A swallow assessment before feeding prevents recurrence.

dx.asthma.note: Variable airflow obstruction (peak flow or spirometry) confirms it; clubbing, a localised wheeze or first onset after 40 in a smoker point elsewhere. Cardiac wheeze from mitral stenosis or heart failure mimics asthma in Uganda.

dx.asthma_exacerbation.note: A silent chest, exhaustion, SpO2 below 92% or a normal or rising PaCO2 mark life-threatening asthma: a quiet chest is worse than a loud one. Stridor is upper-airway obstruction, not asthma.

dx.back_pain_red_flags.note: Saddle numbness, new bladder or bowel disturbance or bilateral leg symptoms need same-day MRI for cauda equina. Fever, weight loss and a gibbus point to spinal TB; cancer history and night pain to metastases or myeloma.

dx.bells_palsy.note: Forehead involvement marks a lower motor neuron lesion; forehead sparing is a stroke until proven otherwise. Test for HIV, and look in the ear for zoster vesicles (Ramsay Hunt) or chronic otitis before calling it Bell palsy.

dx.bipolar.note: Ask about past elevated mood or reduced need for sleep in anyone presenting with depression. A first manic episode needs an organic screen (HIV, syphilis, thyroid, substances, steroids, CNS infection).

dx.bladder_cancer.note: Squamous bladder cancer follows chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection, whose Ugandan foci are patchy (confirm locally); ask where the patient grew up and swam or farmed. Visible haematuria without infection needs imaging and cystoscopy referral.

dx.bowel_obstruction.must_not_miss_reason: Strangulation, ischaemia and perforation develop within hours; needs early surgical review.
dx.bowel_obstruction.note: Sigmoid volvulus, obstructed hernia, adhesions, abdominal TB and colorectal cancer are the Ugandan causes, so examine every hernial orifice. Constant pain, fever, tachycardia or peritonism suggest strangulation.

dx.bph.note: A hard, nodular or asymmetric prostate, bone pain or weight loss points to prostate cancer, which is common and presents late in Ugandan men. Exclude diabetes and urethral stricture as causes of the same symptoms.

dx.bppv.note: Brief spinning vertigo on head movement, confirmed by a positive Dix-Hallpike test, which is not yet a catalogue item. Continuous vertigo, inability to stand, hearing loss or any focal sign is not BPPV.

dx.breast_cancer.note: The examination has no breast item (mass, skin tethering, peau d'orange, nipple change) and there is no breast-imaging test id; both are gaps. Ugandan women commonly present at stage III or IV, and a breast lump in a man also needs assessment.

dx.breathlessness_unexplained.note: Chest signs, JVP and pallor split lung, heart and anaemia causes; deep sighing breathing with clear lungs points to acidosis (DKA, sepsis, renal failure). In HIV, PCP and TB sit alongside bacterial pneumonia.

dx.bronchiectasis.note: Post-TB bronchiectasis is the commonest form in Uganda; recurrent or large haemoptysis needs urgent review. Re-test for active TB (Xpert) before attributing symptoms to bronchiectasis.

dx.brucellosis.note: Ask about livestock and unpasteurised milk in the cattle corridor; the history catalogue records animal exposure but has no dairy item. Spondylitis mimics spinal TB.

dx.burn.note: There is no burn examination item (site, depth, % TBSA, circumferential, face or airway involvement; catalogue gap), so evidence is a single weak proxy and blistering is not used because it equally suggests SJS/TEN or envenoming; record in free text and grade with the TBSA scale. Epilepsy is a common cause of burns in Uganda, and SpO2 reads falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning.

dx.cancer_suspected.note: TB and HIV cause the same wasting, sweats and lymphadenopathy and often coexist, so finding one does not close the other; when TB treatment fails, get tissue (archive, weight loss). Kaposi sarcoma and lymphoma peak in the thirties in Kampala, so a young age is not reassuring.

dx.cardiac_tamponade.must_not_miss_reason: Tamponade causes obstructive shock and cardiac arrest; bedside echo and pericardiocentesis are life-saving.
dx.cardiac_tamponade.note: Beck's triad is often incomplete and clear lungs with a raised JVP and hypotension should prompt a bedside echo. TB pericarditis, often with HIV, is the usual cause here.

dx.cardiogenic_shock.must_not_miss_reason: Mortality is high and rises with every hour of hypoperfusion; treating it as hypovolaemia with large fluid volumes makes it worse.
dx.cardiogenic_shock.note: Causes here include ACS, end-stage cardiomyopathy or valve disease, arrhythmia and myocarditis. Exclude obstructive shock (tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive PE) with bedside ultrasound.

dx.cardiomyopathy.note: Peripartum (last month of pregnancy to five months after delivery), HIV-associated, alcoholic and idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy predominate, with endomyocardial fibrosis in some regions; the catalogue does not yet ask about recent pregnancy. Echo separates it from rheumatic valve disease.

dx.cellulitis.note: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, bullae or systemic toxicity mean necrotising infection until excluded. Interdigital tinea is a common portal of entry; bilateral red legs are rarely cellulitis.

dx.cerebral_toxoplasmosis.must_not_miss_reason: The commonest focal brain lesion in advanced HIV; it responds to treatment and is fatal without it.
dx.cerebral_toxoplasmosis.note: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions with CD4 below 100 support it, and negative toxoplasma IgG makes it unlikely. Where CT is unavailable, clinical response to an empirical trial within two weeks is the practical test; tuberculoma and CNS lymphoma are the mimics.

dx.chest_pain_unexplained.note: ECG early for every new chest pain; exertional, sweaty or breathless pain is ACS until proven otherwise. Tearing pain to the back or an inter-arm BP difference suggests dissection; a rub suggests pericarditis (TB pericarditis is common in HIV).

dx.cholangitis.must_not_miss_reason: Biliary sepsis that progresses to septic shock within hours without antibiotics and drainage.
dx.cholangitis.note: Charcot's triad (fever, right upper quadrant pain, jaundice); added confusion and hypotension (Reynolds) mean suppurative cholangitis needing urgent drainage. Febrile jaundice in Uganda is more often malaria, hepatitis or leptospirosis, so test for malaria as well; Tokyo grading has no source id yet.

dx.cholecystitis.note: Jaundice or confusion with fever means cholangitis until proven otherwise. Amoebic liver abscess and acute hepatitis are the Ugandan mimics of right upper quadrant pain; pigment stones are common in sickle cell disease.

dx.cholera.must_not_miss_reason: Profuse watery diarrhoea can kill from dehydration within hours, and one case is a notifiable outbreak signal.
dx.cholera.note: Notify every suspected case under IDSR and confirm by stool culture; the catalogue has no cholera rapid test (an addition for the CSO to consider). Fever and bloody stool are unusual and point elsewhere.

dx.chronic_pulmonary_aspergillosis.note: Often misdiagnosed as smear-negative or relapsed TB after TB treatment; its defining fact (previous TB) is restricted and not offered as evidence, so the remaining atoms are non-specific (CSO to decide). Xpert-negative haemoptysis with a persisting cavity should prompt Aspergillus IgG (not yet in the test catalogue), and massive haemoptysis from an aspergilloma is life-threatening.

dx.ckd.note: Chronicity needs reduced eGFR or kidney damage for over three months, or small kidneys on ultrasound; until then treat a raised creatinine as AKI. Leading Ugandan causes are hypertension, diabetes, HIV-associated nephropathy, glomerulonephritis and herbal nephrotoxins.

dx.colorectal_cancer.note: Colorectal cancer in sub-Saharan Africa presents younger and later than in the West (CSO to confirm local data), so a young age should not stop a rectal examination. Haemorrhoids do not explain anaemia or weight loss.

dx.confusion_unexplained.note: Glucose, oxygen and temperature first; infection (sepsis, malaria, meningitis) is the leading cause. Hypoglycaemia in Uganda is often non-diabetic (malaria, sepsis, alcohol, liver failure), and a gradual stable course suggests dementia rather than delirium.

dx.conjunctivitis.note: Reduced vision, photophobia, marked pain or an abnormal pupil mean keratitis, uveitis or acute glaucoma, not conjunctivitis: refer the same day. Zoster on the forehead or nose tip threatens the eye.

dx.copd.note: In Uganda biomass (cooking) smoke and previous TB cause much fixed airflow obstruction in non-smokers, especially women; there is no biomass-exposure question yet. Clubbing is not a feature of COPD and points to cancer, bronchiectasis or fibrosis.

dx.copd_exacerbation.note: Hypercapnia risk: get a blood gas early (BTS). Exclude pneumothorax, pneumonia, PE and heart failure as the trigger or the mimic.

dx.cord_compression.must_not_miss_reason: Paralysis and sphincter loss become permanent if decompression or treatment is delayed; function at treatment predicts outcome.
dx.cord_compression.note: Pott disease and metastatic cancer (prostate, breast, myeloma) are the leading Ugandan causes, with lymphoma and TB in HIV. Cauda equina gives saddle numbness and bladder symptoms with lower motor neuron signs, not a sensory level.

dx.cough_unexplained.note: Cough for two weeks or more, or any cough in a person with HIV, needs TB testing (Xpert). ACE-inhibitor cough and heart failure are the common non-infective causes.

dx.covid19.note: WHO severity (SpO2 below 90% or respiratory distress is severe) decides escalation of care. Test for malaria in any febrile patient in Uganda.

dx.cryptococcal_meningitis.must_not_miss_reason: The leading cause of adult meningitis in Ugandan advanced HIV; raised pressure kills and is relieved by therapeutic LP.
dx.cryptococcal_meningitis.note: Neck stiffness is often absent, so its absence is not used against; record the CSF opening pressure. A positive blood CrAg without symptoms still needs an LP.

dx.cvst.must_not_miss_reason: Protean and easily missed; untreated it causes venous infarction, haemorrhage and death, and it needs specific venous imaging and anticoagulation.
dx.cvst.note: Risks are pregnancy and the puerperium, hormonal contraception, dehydration, ear or sinus infection, HIV and sickle cell; pregnancy status and contraception are not yet catalogue items. CT or MR venography is needed because plain CT is often normal.

dx.delirium.note: Acute onset with fluctuating attention defines it; the 4AT is not yet in the catalogue, so AMTS and observed behaviour stand in. Delirium on top of dementia is common and still needs a full search for the cause.

dx.dementia.note: Diagnose only after delirium, depression and reversible causes (HIV, syphilis, hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, subdural haematoma) are excluded; an acute or fluctuating change is delirium until proven otherwise. HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder affects younger adults.

dx.dental_abscess.note: Floor-of-mouth swelling, trismus, drooling, difficulty swallowing or stridor suggest Ludwig angina, an airway emergency. Check for diabetes and HIV in deep or recurrent infection.

dx.depression.note: Depression is common in Ugandan primary care and more common in people with HIV; always ask about self-harm. Exclude hypothyroidism, anaemia, HIV and medicine effects before attributing fatigue to depression.

dx.diabetes_in_pregnancy.must_not_miss_reason: Reason awaiting the CSO: the pack marks it must-not-miss without one (MS-NCD-DM-PACK-001 Phase 5).
dx.diabetes_in_pregnancy.note: Specialised multidisciplinary care, with retinal and kidney assessment when antenatal care starts (WHO 2025). ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated; lipid-lowering medicines are, in most circumstances, stopped (ADA).

dx.diabetic_foot.note: Not must-not-miss because it includes uninfected neuropathic ulcers: a positive probe-to-bone test or an ulcer over bone for more than two weeks escalates to dx.osteomyelitis, and spreading or gas-forming infection to dx.necrotising_soft_tissue or dx.sepsis. Foot pulses and temperature separate ischaemic from neuropathic ulcers, and late presentation after self or traditional treatment is common.

dx.diabetic_kidney_disease.note: One result is not kidney disease: it needs 3 months and, for albumin, 2 of 3 samples. Exercise, fever, infection, menstruation and very high glucose raise albumin transiently. Creatinine-based eGFR overestimated kidney function in Ugandan adults. Blood on the strip, a nephrotic picture or a fast fall in eGFR points to another cause: refer.

dx.diabetic_neuropathy.note: A diagnosis of exclusion: vitamin B12 deficiency (long-term metformin), alcohol, medicines, hypothyroidism and kidney disease first. Sudden, one-sided or mainly motor loss is not this: refer. Half of cases have no symptoms.

dx.diabetic_retinopathy.note: No 'against' evidence is listed: a normal undilated direct ophthalmoscopy misses most retinopathy. Vision worse than 6/12 or any visual symptom is referred whatever the grade. A rapid fall in HbA1c can worsen retinopathy at first.

dx.diarrhoea_unexplained.note: Grade dehydration first; rice-water stool in an outbreak area is cholera until tested and is notifiable. Diarrhoea for over a month is a WHO stage 3 HIV criterion.

dx.dic.note: Always secondary: sepsis, severe malaria, obstetric haemorrhage, snakebite, trauma or malignancy; the 20-minute whole blood clotting test is the bedside screen where no coagulation lab is available. Fever with bleeding and an exposure history needs VHF isolation before sampling.

dx.dka.must_not_miss_reason: Fatal within hours without fluids, insulin and potassium management; the abdominal pain and vomiting are easily mistaken for a surgical abdomen or gastroenteritis.
dx.dka.note: Look for the precipitant: infection including malaria, missed insulin (often cost or supply), or new diabetes. Ketosis-prone type 2 is common in African adults, so DKA does not fix the diabetes type.

dx.dm_type1.note: Ketosis-prone type 2 and atypical lean diabetes are common in young Ugandan adults, and C-peptide and antibodies are rarely available, so ketosis alone does not make this type 1. Prefer dx.dm_type_unknown until the course (insulin need off treatment) settles the type.

dx.dm_type2.note: A working type label should not reach the problem list: lean type 2 and ketosis-prone type 2 are common in sub-Saharan Africa, so DKA at presentation does not exclude it. Screen for complications (feet, eyes, kidneys) at diagnosis, since many present late.

dx.dm_type_unknown.note: The preferred label while the type is unclear (young, lean, or ketotic at presentation). A single random glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or more with classic symptoms is diagnostic; without symptoms confirm with a second test.

dx.drug_induced_liver_injury.must_not_miss_reason: Continuing the culprit (anti-TB drugs, nevirapine, herbal remedies) can progress to acute liver failure; stopping it is the key action.
dx.drug_induced_liver_injury.note: Anti-TB drugs, nevirapine or efavirenz, co-trimoxazole and herbal remedies are the main Ugandan culprits, but those medicine answers are restricted and so only feed the ask list here. Exclude viral hepatitis (HBV, HEV) before attributing the injury to a drug.

dx.drug_rash.note: Before accepting a simple drug rash, look for the danger signs of SJS/TEN and DRESS: mucosal involvement, blisters, skin pain, fever, facial swelling, lymphadenopathy, raised transaminases or eosinophilia. A rash on nevirapine or abacavir needs the ART clinician the same day.

dx.dvt.must_not_miss_reason: Untreated proximal DVT embolises to the lungs; anticoagulation prevents fatal PE.
dx.dvt.note: Wells score with D-dimer or leg Doppler decides; in Uganda HIV, TB and the postpartum state are common added risks. Cellulitis, pyomyositis and a ruptured Baker's cyst mimic it.

dx.dysentery.note: Shigella causes epidemics and amoebiasis can perforate the colon or seed a liver abscess; stool microscopy separates them. Bloody diarrhoea for weeks with weight loss needs colonic assessment for TB, cancer or inflammatory bowel disease.

dx.dyslipidaemia.note: A laboratory diagnosis, so the label waits for a lipid panel. Look for secondary causes: diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, alcohol and antiretrovirals (protease inhibitors, efavirenz).

dx.dyspepsia.note: Alarm features argue against settling on dyspepsia and toward endoscopy for gastric or oesophageal cancer. Epigastric discomfort in someone with cardiac risk factors needs an ECG before this label.

dx.eclampsia.must_not_miss_reason: A leading cause of maternal death in Uganda; recurrent fits, stroke and fetal death follow within hours without treatment and delivery.
dx.eclampsia.note: Any fit in a pregnant or recently delivered woman is eclampsia until proven otherwise, even with known epilepsy; cerebral malaria and meningitis are the local look-alikes and can coexist. Pregnancy status and gestation are not captured fields.

dx.ectopic_pregnancy.must_not_miss_reason: Rupture causes haemorrhagic shock and is a leading cause of maternal death in Uganda; a pregnancy test and surgery save lives.
dx.ectopic_pregnancy.note: A pregnancy test in every woman of reproductive age with abdominal or pelvic pain or collapse is the core rule (archive, abdominal pain). Vaginal bleeding is a restricted history item and is not used here; the pelvic-pain bleeding red flag carries it.

dx.encephalitis.must_not_miss_reason: HSV encephalitis is treatable and causes death or lasting brain damage when antiviral treatment is delayed.
dx.encephalitis.note: Behaviour or speech change with fever and seizures suggests HSV; CSF HSV PCR is not a separate catalogue test. Exclude cerebral malaria and hypoglycaemia first, and consider rabies or trypanosomiasis with the right exposure.

dx.epilepsy.note: Needs recurrent unprovoked seizures; do not label after a provoked seizure (hypoglycaemia, alcohol withdrawal, CNS infection, eclampsia). Neurocysticercosis and post-infective scarring are leading causes of adult-onset epilepsy in Uganda.

dx.fatigue_unexplained.note: HIV, TB and anaemia come first in Uganda; look for fever, night sweats, weight loss, nodes and pallor before any functional or mood explanation. Zidovudine-containing ART causes anaemia.

dx.febrile_neutropenia.must_not_miss_reason: Can progress to septic shock within hours; empirical antibiotics should not wait for the blood count.
dx.febrile_neutropenia.note: Recent chemotherapy is not a structured history item, so ask directly; neutrophils below 0.5 x10^9/L define it. Drug-induced neutropenia (for example co-trimoxazole or zidovudine) also occurs in people with HIV.

dx.fever_unexplained.note: Every fever in Uganda gets a malaria test; a negative test with persisting fever widens the search to TB, HIV, typhoid, endocarditis and brucellosis. Sick contacts, burials or an outbreak area trigger the IDSR VHF case definition.

dx.fracture.note: A fracture after minor trauma, or bone pain at night, needs a search for metastases, myeloma or TB. Pelvic and femoral fractures can bleed enough to cause shock.

dx.gastric_cancer.note: H. pylori infection is not a captured history item (archive gap). Dyspepsia with weight loss, vomiting, anaemia or melaena warrants endoscopy rather than repeated empirical treatment.

dx.gastroenteritis.note: Malaria often presents with vomiting and diarrhoea in adults: test. Diarrhoea beyond 14 days, especially with HIV, needs stool microscopy for opportunistic parasites.

dx.gbs.must_not_miss_reason: Respiratory and bulbar failure and autonomic instability can develop within hours to days; early immunotherapy and monitoring change outcome.
dx.gbs.note: Areflexia is central to the diagnosis but reflexes and power are not yet catalogue items; a sensory level, early sphincter loss or fever at onset point elsewhere. Look-alikes include hypokalaemia, cord compression, myasthenia and organophosphate intermediate syndrome.

dx.gestational_diabetes.note: Offered only in a pregnant patient, on results from this pregnancy. One value is enough under WHO 2013. HbA1c is not used. WHO is revising these criteria (REF-DM-PREG-REVISION): the reference entries are versioned. After the birth, re-test at 6 to 12 weeks and then at least every 3 years.

dx.gi_bleed_unexplained.must_not_miss_reason: Upper or lower GI bleeding can exsanguinate within hours; source and haemodynamics decide the next hour.
dx.gi_bleed_unexplained.note: Haemodynamics before the source. Varices from schistosomal periportal fibrosis or hepatitis B cirrhosis are common in Uganda alongside peptic ulcer, and a large spleen is the clue.

dx.giant_cell_arteritis.must_not_miss_reason: Can cause sudden permanent blindness in one or both eyes; treatment on suspicion prevents it.
dx.giant_cell_arteritis.note: Essentially never under 50 and apparently less common in sub-Saharan Africa; jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and temporal artery findings are not yet catalogue items. Visual symptoms need same-day treatment and eye review.

dx.gord.note: Retrosternal burning in a person with cardiac risk factors needs cardiac causes weighed first. Dysphagia or weight loss is oesophageal cancer until endoscopy in the East African oesophageal cancer corridor, and odynophagia in advanced HIV suggests oesophageal candidiasis.

dx.gout.note: A hot swollen joint needs aspiration for crystals and culture: gout and septic arthritis coexist, and serum urate can be normal during a flare. Thiazides and kidney disease are common Ugandan drivers.

dx.haemolytic_anaemia.note: Malaria is the commonest cause in Uganda; G6PD deficiency (oxidant drugs such as primaquine and dapsone, fava beans, infection), sickle cell disease and autoimmune haemolysis are the others to seek. G6PD, Coombs and LDH are not yet in the test catalogue, and pale stools do not exclude haemolysis because cholestasis can coexist (pigment stones, malarial hepatitis).

dx.haemoptysis_unexplained.note: After treated TB, new haemoptysis may be post-TB lung disease or chronic pulmonary aspergillosis rather than relapse: test (Xpert and culture) before re-treating. Mitral stenosis from rheumatic heart disease is a Ugandan cause.

dx.hcc.note: HBV-related HCC in Uganda arises in younger patients and without cirrhosis, and undiagnosed HBV is common, so a hard or nodular liver warrants AFP and ultrasound without a known liver history (archive, jaundice). Amoebic liver abscess is the tender, febrile look-alike.

dx.head_injury.note: No anticoagulant is on the medicine list and there is no mechanism-of-injury field; ask both in free text. Intoxication does not explain a falling GCS or unequal pupils, and the cervical spine needs clearing.

dx.headache_unexplained.note: Red flags first: thunderclap onset, fever or neck stiffness, focal signs, papilloedema, new headache after 50 and immunosuppression. In people with HIV a subacute headache is cryptococcal meningitis until a CrAg is negative.

dx.heart_block.must_not_miss_reason: Complete heart block causes syncope, cardiac arrest and sudden death; pacing or chronotropic support is time-critical.

options: adverse features (shock, syncope, ischaemia or heart failure)

dx.heart_block.note: Reversible causes include inferior MI, hyperkalaemia and rate-slowing drugs (beta-blockers, digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem); the medicines list names atenolol only. Stokes-Adams attacks can be mistaken for seizures.

dx.heart_failure.note: Ugandan heart failure is younger and mostly hypertensive, rheumatic, peripartum or other cardiomyopathy (including HIV), not ischaemic: name the cause with echo. Exclude severe anaemia, which gives high-output failure.

dx.heart_failure_acute.must_not_miss_reason: Acute pulmonary oedema causes hypoxaemic respiratory failure and death within hours unless oxygenation, ventilation and the trigger are treated.
dx.heart_failure_acute.note: Find the trigger: ACS, new AF, hypertensive emergency, infection, stopped medicines, severe anaemia, or peripartum cardiomyopathy in a young woman. Cold peripheries or a low systolic pressure mean cardiogenic shock.

dx.heat_stroke.must_not_miss_reason: Brain, muscle, kidney and clotting injury accumulate with every minute of hyperthermia; cooling must begin at once.
dx.heat_stroke.note: In Uganda a hot, confused patient has cerebral malaria, meningitis or sepsis far more often than heat stroke; test for malaria and consider LP even when exertion or heat exposure is clear. Stimulant or anticholinergic toxicity and thyroid storm are the other hyperthermic look-alikes.

dx.hepatic_encephalopathy.must_not_miss_reason: Marks decompensation and usually has a treatable precipitant (GI bleed, SBP or other infection, hypokalaemia); grades III-IV threaten the airway.
dx.hepatic_encephalopathy.note: Always seek the precipitant: GI bleed, SBP or other infection, constipation, dehydration or diuretics, hypokalaemia, sedatives. Exclude hypoglycaemia, Wernicke encephalopathy and subdural haematoma in drinkers; a raised ammonia does not confirm or grade HE, and a normal value should prompt a search for another cause.

dx.hepatitis_acute_viral.note: Confusion, bleeding or a rising INR mean acute liver failure, and hepatitis E in pregnancy is often severe: escalate. In Uganda exclude malaria, drug and herbal liver injury and, in outbreaks, yellow fever or VHF.

dx.hepatitis_b_chronic.note: Mostly silent: the label needs HBsAg positive for six months or more, and staging (ALT, platelets or APRI, viral load where available) decides treatment. HCC arises without cirrhosis in hepatitis B, so surveillance applies.

dx.hepatitis_c_chronic.note: A positive antibody needs HCV RNA to confirm chronic infection, and the catalogue has no HCV RNA test. Less common than hepatitis B in Uganda but curable, so test anyone with unexplained liver disease.

dx.herpes_zoster.note: Zoster in an adult under 50 in Uganda warrants an HIV test (WHO stage 2). Eye involvement needs urgent eye review, and multidermatomal or disseminated disease suggests immunosuppression.

dx.hhs.must_not_miss_reason: Profound dehydration with high mortality, especially in older adults; thrombosis and overly rapid osmolality shifts add harm.
dx.hhs.note: Often the first presentation of type 2 diabetes; mixed DKA and HHS is common, so measure ketones even when the picture looks hyperosmolar. Many glucometers read only "HI" above their ceiling; calculate osmolality from sodium, urea and glucose.

dx.hiv.note: The label needs a confirmed result under the national testing algorithm; offer testing to every adult admitted with an unexplained illness. Being on ART does not exclude advanced disease: record viral load and adherence.

dx.hiv_acute.note: Rapid antibody tests can be negative in the window period; with a compatible illness and recent exposure, repeat testing or HIV RNA is needed. Viral load is very high at this stage, so partner testing and counselling matter.

dx.hiv_advanced.note: WHO definition in adults: CD4 below 200 or WHO stage 3 or 4; people re-engaging after ART interruption or with treatment failure qualify for assessment. High early mortality: apply the WHO advanced-disease package and expect more than one active diagnosis, each lethal one (cryptococcal and TB meningitis, PCP, toxoplasmosis, sepsis) carrying its own must-not-miss flag.

dx.hookworm_helminth.note: Hookworm causes occult blood loss and iron deficiency, so pallor and fatigue rather than visible bleeding; stool microscopy decides. Iron deficiency in an older adult still needs a GI source excluded even when ova are found.

dx.hypercalcaemia.note: Malignancy (myeloma, breast, lung and other squamous cancers) and primary hyperparathyroidism are the common causes; TB and other granulomatous disease are a Ugandan consideration. Correct calcium for albumin; PTH is not in the test catalogue yet.

dx.hyperemesis.note: A first-trimester diagnosis of exclusion; fever, diarrhoea or marked pain point to malaria, UTI or gastroenteritis instead. Molar pregnancy and thyrotoxicosis are look-alikes, and prolonged vomiting risks Wernicke encephalopathy.

dx.hyperglycaemia_unconfirmed.note: A holding label for a raised glucose that is not yet a diagnosis: acute illness, steroids, or one value without symptoms. It carries a follow-up test into the Plan so the result is not lost. Never added to the problem list.

dx.hyperkalaemia.must_not_miss_reason: Causes bradyarrhythmia and cardiac arrest without warning symptoms.
dx.hyperkalaemia.note: Record an ECG as soon as the result is known; haemolysed or delayed samples read falsely high, but ECG changes are acted on regardless. AKI from malaria, sepsis and dehydration is the commonest route on the Ugandan ward.

dx.hypernatraemia.note: Almost always water loss without access to water: the bedbound, confused or older patient, or one with HHS or diarrhoea. Large volumes of dilute urine raise diabetes insipidus (after head injury, or from hypercalcaemia).

dx.hypertension.note: One raised clinic reading is not a diagnosis: confirm on at least two separate days before labelling. In a young patient look for a secondary cause, kidney disease first.

dx.hypertensive_crisis.must_not_miss_reason: Hypertensive emergency with acute organ damage (encephalopathy, stroke, pulmonary oedema, dissection, eclampsia, AKI) kills within hours without controlled BP reduction.
dx.hypertensive_crisis.note: Severe BP without acute organ damage (urgency) is not an emergency and rapid lowering causes harm (stroke, myocardial or renal ischaemia); the grade is set by acute organ damage, not by the number. In a pregnant or postpartum woman treat it as severe pre-eclampsia until proven otherwise.

dx.hypoglycaemia_dm.must_not_miss_reason: Causes seizures, brain injury and death within minutes to hours and is reversed immediately by glucose.
dx.hypoglycaemia_dm.note: Glibenclamide hypoglycaemia is prolonged and recurs, especially with kidney impairment or poor intake, so it needs longer observation than insulin-related episodes. The examination classifier grades levels 1 and 2 from the glucose value; level 3 (needing help from another person) is clinical, with no glucose threshold, so the clinician sets it.

dx.hypoglycaemia_no_dm.must_not_miss_reason: Causes seizures, brain injury and death within hours, and usually signals a serious cause (severe malaria, sepsis, liver failure, adrenal insufficiency).
dx.hypoglycaemia_no_dm.note: In Uganda the usual causes are severe malaria (and quinine), sepsis, alcohol, liver failure and starvation; adrenal insufficiency is the treatable cause to seek in TB and advanced HIV, and unlabelled sulfonylurea in herbal or borrowed medicines is worth asking about. The examination classifier grades levels 1 and 2 from the glucose value; level 3 (needing help from another person) is clinical, with no glucose threshold, so the clinician sets it.

dx.hypokalaemia.note: Diarrhoea (including cholera and HIV-related diarrhoea), diuretics, refeeding and amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis are the main routes; amphotericin has no medicine answer. Check magnesium, since low magnesium keeps potassium low.

dx.hyponatraemia.note: Assess volume status first; thiazides, diarrhoeal losses, SIADH from pneumonia, TB meningitis or intracranial disease, and adrenal insufficiency are common routes here. Severe symptoms (seizures, reduced consciousness) and over-rapid correction (osmotic demyelination) carry the danger, graded by severity rather than must-not-miss; urine sodium and osmolality are not in the test catalogue yet.

dx.hypothermia_accidental.must_not_miss_reason: Moderate and severe hypothermia cause arrhythmia and cardiac arrest; rewarming and careful handling must start at once.
dx.hypothermia_accidental.note: Accidental hypothermia is uncommon in Uganda; a low temperature is more often sepsis, hypoglycaemia, hypothyroidism or intoxication, so look for them before settling on exposure. Many ward thermometers cannot read low temperatures reliably; confirm with a low-reading core thermometer.

dx.hypothermia_unexplained.note: Confirm with a low-reading core thermometer. On a Ugandan ward, hypothermia is more often sepsis, hypoglycaemia, advanced HIV or wasting than cold exposure; cold exposure and sedative use are not yet catalogue items, so ask directly.

dx.hypothyroidism.note: Ask about previous thyroid surgery or radioiodine, which the thyroid-disease history answer captures only loosely. It mimics depression and cognitive decline, so check TSH before settling on either.

dx.hypovolaemic_shock.must_not_miss_reason: Shock from haemorrhage or fluid loss is fatal within hours unless volume is restored and the source controlled.
dx.hypovolaemic_shock.note: Find the source: GI bleed, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, trauma, postpartum haemorrhage, ruptured spleen, cholera or severe gastroenteritis. Young patients hold their BP until late (tachycardia and cool peripheries come first), and a raised JVP does not exclude mixed shock such as bleeding with tamponade or tension pneumothorax.

dx.infective_endocarditis.must_not_miss_reason: Curable if found but destroys valves and embolises; rheumatic heart disease makes it common in young Ugandan adults.
dx.infective_endocarditis.note: Take three sets of blood cultures before any antibiotic; prior antibiotics explain many culture-negative cases here. The history catalogue has no rheumatic heart disease or prosthetic valve item, so ask directly.

dx.influenza.note: Abrupt fever with myalgia during a season or outbreak; secondary bacterial pneumonia is the main complication. Malaria must be tested first in Uganda.

dx.intermediate_hyperglycaemia.note: WHO bands. ADA starts impaired fasting glucose at 5.6 mmol/L and adds HbA1c 5.7 to 6.4%; WHO does neither. A fasting value in this range is followed by an OGTT. Re-test every year.

dx.interstitial_lung_disease.note: Uncommon in Uganda and easily confused with post-TB fibrosis, heart failure and PCP; fine late inspiratory crackles with clubbing are the pointer. Silicosis in miners carries a high TB risk.

dx.iron_deficiency_anaemia.note: Hookworm, menstrual loss and pregnancy are common sources in Uganda, but in men and postmenopausal women the gut must be investigated for cancer. Ferritin rises with inflammation, so a normal ferritin during infection does not exclude iron deficiency; the over-the-counter pain-killer answer stands in for NSAID exposure until the medicine list has an NSAID item.

dx.jaundice_unexplained.note: Separate haemolytic (malaria, sickle cell), hepatocellular and obstructive causes; fever with jaundice includes severe malaria, hepatitis, cholangitis, leptospirosis and yellow fever or VHF during alerts. TB drugs and herbal medicines are common causes of drug-induced liver injury.

dx.kaposi_sarcoma.note: Among the commonest male cancers in Kampala (CSO to verify against the latest Kampala Cancer Registry report), peaking in the early to mid thirties; pulmonary and GI disease cause haemoptysis and occult bleeding and are mistaken for TB (archive). Confirm by biopsy, since bacillary angiomatosis looks the same.

dx.leptospirosis.note: Floods, rice or sugar-cane farming and rodent exposure are the clues; conjunctival suffusion without discharge and calf tenderness are the specific signs. The catalogue has no leptospira test, so the diagnosis rests on the picture once malaria is excluded.

dx.leukaemia.must_not_miss_reason: Acute leukaemia kills through bleeding and neutropenic sepsis within days, and a full blood count separates it; chronic forms are not time-critical.
dx.leukaemia.note: Fatigue with bruising, bleeding or recurrent infection is acute leukaemia until a full blood count and film say otherwise (archive, fatigue). Massive splenomegaly here is often hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly or visceral leishmaniasis, but chronic myeloid leukaemia is a common cause.

dx.liver_abscess.note: Ultrasound decides; amoebic (young men, often no recent dysentery) and pyogenic (biliary source, diabetes) abscesses look alike. Jaundice is uncommon in amoebic abscess and suggests a biliary cause.

dx.liver_cirrhosis.note: Hepatitis B and alcohol dominate in Uganda; S. mansoni periportal fibrosis gives portal hypertension and varices with preserved liver function and is not cirrhosis. Child-Pugh needs bilirubin, albumin and INR from results; compensated cirrhosis can have a normal examination.

dx.liver_disease_unexplained.note: Hepatitis B, alcohol, hepatosplenic schistosomiasis (lakeshore and Nile fishing communities) and drug or herbal injury are the main Ugandan causes. A large spleen with preserved liver function suggests schistosomal periportal fibrosis.

dx.low_back_pain.note: Non-specific mechanical back pain needs no imaging once red flags are asked and absent. In Uganda TB, cancer and brucellosis are the causes that red flags protect against.

dx.lung_abscess_empyema.note: Tap any effusion with pneumonia that is not settling: pus, low pH or organisms on Gram stain mean empyema and a drain. Cavitating TB and cavitating carcinoma are the mimics.

dx.lung_cancer.note: TB dominates and must be excluded first, but a second empirical TB course without bacteriological proof is a known local error; scar carcinoma after TB and cancer in never-smokers both occur (archive, cough). Diagnosis is often late here.

dx.lymphadenopathy_unexplained.note: Localised nodes: examine the drainage area; generalised nodes: HIV, TB, lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma, syphilis. Asymmetric, matted, fast-growing nodes or nodes with fever and weight loss need aspiration: TB lymphadenitis is the commonest cause in HIV.

dx.lymphatic_filariasis.note: Endemic in specific foci rather than nationwide; podoconiosis is the main non-filarial mimic and has no term of its own. Filarial antigen tests are not in the catalogue, so a night blood film is the available option.

dx.lymphoma.note: In Uganda lymphoma is repeatedly treated as TB, and the two coexist in HIV: lymphadenopathy with wasting that does not respond to TB treatment means biopsy, not a second TB course (archive, weight loss; a DDX rule for nodes on TB treatment is proposed). Aspirate cytology can miss lymphoma; excision biopsy is preferred where it can be done.

dx.malaria_cerebral.must_not_miss_reason: Coma with parasitaemia has high mortality; treatment and glucose correction cannot wait for other results.
dx.malaria_cerebral.note: Needs parasitaemia plus coma with other causes excluded: check glucose and consider LP, because bacterial meningitis coexists. Incidental parasitaemia is common in holoendemic Uganda, so a positive smear does not close the differential.

dx.malaria_severe.must_not_miss_reason: High mortality that falls with prompt parenteral treatment; any single WHO severity criterion makes it an emergency.
dx.malaria_severe.note: WHO laboratory criteria (hyperparasitaemia, haemoglobin, creatinine, lactate, bicarbonate) are not bedside findings, and the glucose atom uses the 3.0 mmol/L reference where the WHO criterion is below 2.2 mmol/L (CSO to confirm). Bacterial sepsis coexists often enough that blood cultures belong in the work-up.

dx.malaria_uncomplicated.note: Any WHO or UCG danger sign (prostration, impaired consciousness, repeated vomiting, jaundice, dark urine) reclassifies as severe malaria. A negative RDT with persisting fever needs a smear and a search for another cause, not presumptive treatment.

dx.malaria_unconfirmed.note: Working label only: WHO and UCG require a parasitological test before treatment wherever one is available. Should be replaced by a confirmed or excluded diagnosis once the RDT or smear is back.

dx.megaloblastic_anaemia.note: Posterior column loss, neuropathy or cognitive change point to B12 rather than folate and can occur without anaemia. Zidovudine and alcohol cause macrocytosis without megaloblastosis; pregnancy and poor diet drive folate deficiency.

dx.meningitis_bacterial.must_not_miss_reason: Death or lasting disability rises with each hour of delayed antibiotics.
dx.meningitis_bacterial.note: Do not delay antibiotics for LP or CT; absent neck stiffness does not exclude it (NICE NG240). In HIV, cryptococcal and TB meningitis are commoner than bacterial and meningism is often absent.

dx.meningitis_unexplained.must_not_miss_reason: Bacterial, cryptococcal and TB meningitis kill quickly and each needs different urgent treatment; delay to antimicrobials while awaiting LP or CT raises mortality.
dx.meningitis_unexplained.note: Neck stiffness is often absent in HIV-associated (cryptococcal, TB) meningitis, so its absence is not evidence against. Serum CrAg for everyone with HIV; a non-blanching rash is meningococcal disease.

dx.methanol_poisoning.must_not_miss_reason: Untreated methanol causes severe metabolic acidosis, permanent blindness and death; antidote and dialysis are time-dependent.
dx.methanol_poisoning.note: Ugandan outbreaks follow adulterated waragi and sachet spirits; several patients from one drinking source is a public-health event to report. Symptoms start 12 to 24 hours after drinking, and levels are rarely available, so an unexplained high anion-gap acidosis with visual symptoms is enough to act on.

dx.migraine.note: Diagnose a recurrent pattern only after red flags are cleared; a first, worst or thunderclap headache is not migraine. Throbbing quality, photophobia and aura are not yet history fields; ask about analgesic overuse.

dx.mpox.note: Clade Ib has spread in Uganda since 2024, mainly through sexual and household contact; lesions at one stage, often genital or perianal, with lymphadenopathy separate it from chickenpox. Isolate pending PCR, notify under IDSR and test for HIV and syphilis.

dx.msk_chest_pain.note: A diagnosis of exclusion once ACS, PE, dissection and pneumothorax are considered; chest-wall tenderness is not yet a catalogue item and does not exclude ACS. Zoster can cause pain days before the rash.

dx.myasthenia.note: Fatigable ptosis, diplopia and bulbar or limb weakness with normal pupils and sensation; breathing or swallowing weakness is a crisis. Acetylcholine-receptor antibody testing is not in the test catalogue.

dx.myeloma.note: Serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains are not in the test catalogue (gap); anaemia, a high ESR, raised calcium and renal impairment together should prompt them. In Uganda a collapsed vertebra is TB as often as myeloma or metastasis.

dx.myxoedema_coma.must_not_miss_reason: Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation and hyponatraemia progress to death without thyroid hormone and supportive care; it is often mistaken for sepsis or stroke.
dx.myxoedema_coma.note: Rare; usually untreated or undertreated hypothyroidism tipped over by infection, cold or sedatives, so look for the precipitant. Coexisting adrenal insufficiency must be considered until cortisol is known.

dx.necrotising_soft_tissue.must_not_miss_reason: Mortality rises with every hour before surgical debridement, and early signs are subtle.
dx.necrotising_soft_tissue.note: Pain out of proportion to the visible signs is the early clue; crepitus, bullae and skin necrosis are late. Surgical exploration, not imaging, confirms it; there is no structured item for limb crepitus.

dx.nephritic_syndrome.note: A rapidly rising creatinine, oliguria or haemoptysis suggests rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, which needs same-day specialist review. Post-streptococcal disease after a throat or skin infection is the classic young-adult cause; also consider lupus, hepatitis B or C, HIV and endocarditis.

dx.nephrotic_syndrome.note: Ugandan causes include HIV-associated nephropathy, hepatitis B membranous disease, diabetes, and schistosomiasis-, malaria- and herbal-associated glomerulopathy. Heavy proteinuria with a normal JVP separates it from cardiac oedema at the bedside.

dx.neurocysticercosis.note: A leading cause of adult-onset seizures in pig-rearing areas of Uganda; CT showing cysts or calcified lesions decides. Cysticercus serology is not in the catalogue, and in HIV toxoplasmosis and tuberculoma must be excluded first.

dx.obesity.note: Waist measures add to BMI, which can under-read cardiometabolic risk. Screen for diabetes, hypertension and sleep apnoea.

dx.obstructive_uropathy.note: Bilateral hydronephrosis in a Ugandan woman is advanced cervical cancer until proven otherwise; in men prostate disease and urethral stricture, and in both Schistosoma haematobium. Ultrasound decides, and relieving obstruction comes before other AKI work-up.

dx.oedema_unexplained.note: Urine protein and the JVP split renal, cardiac and hepatic causes first; one painful swollen leg is a DVT question. Calcium-channel blockers cause ankle oedema, and endomyocardial fibrosis and TB pericarditis are Ugandan cardiac causes.

dx.oesophageal_cancer.note: Uganda lies in the East African oesophageal squamous-cancer corridor and patients are often under 50, so age does not reassure; progressive dysphagia to solids with weight loss is the story (archive, GI bleeding). In HIV, oesophageal candidiasis is the commoner cause of painful swallowing.

dx.oesophageal_candidiasis.note: A WHO stage 4 condition; painful swallowing with oral thrush in HIV is usually treated empirically. OGD is for failure to respond, where CMV or HSV ulcers, Kaposi sarcoma and oesophageal cancer are the alternatives.

options: with tendon, nerve or vessel injury

dx.open_wound.note: The examination has no wound item (site, length, depth, contamination, bite) and the history has no tetanus-immunisation or mechanism field; these are free text. Ask about animal or human bites, which need rabies exposure assessment.

dx.opioid_sedative_toxicity.must_not_miss_reason: Respiratory depression leads to hypoxic arrest; it is reversible with airway support and, for opioids, an antagonist.
dx.opioid_sedative_toxicity.note: Tramadol and codeine are sold without prescription, and pinpoint pupils cannot yet be recorded (gap). Injecting-drug use is a restricted social item and is not used as evidence here; ask it in private.

dx.oral_candidiasis.note: Persistent oral thrush in an adult without inhaled steroids, recent antibiotics or diabetes is a WHO stage 3 condition, and any unexplained episode warrants an HIV test. Pain on swallowing suggests oesophageal involvement.

dx.organophosphate_poisoning.must_not_miss_reason: Bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm and respiratory muscle paralysis cause death within hours; antidote and airway care are urgent.
dx.organophosphate_poisoning.note: Pinpoint pupils cannot be recorded (pupil size has no reference) and there is no pesticide-exposure question; both are catalogue gaps. Watch for the intermediate syndrome (neck-flexor and proximal weakness, respiratory failure) one to four days after apparent recovery.

dx.orthostatic_hypotension.note: Confirmed by a sustained fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing. In Uganda the usual causes are antihypertensives and diuretics, volume loss, and diabetic or HIV-related autonomic neuropathy; exclude GI bleeding.

dx.osteoarthritis.note: A clinical diagnosis in older adults with use-related pain and brief morning stiffness. A hot swollen joint is not osteoarthritis until septic arthritis and crystals are excluded.

dx.osteomyelitis.note: X-ray changes lag 10 to 14 days, and a foot ulcer that probes to bone is osteomyelitis until shown otherwise. In sickle cell disease Salmonella is common, and bone pain with fever must not be assumed to be a crisis.

dx.otitis_media_acute.note: A clinical diagnosis on otoscopy. Headache, neck stiffness, facial palsy or post-auricular swelling suggest mastoiditis or intracranial spread; chronic discharge beyond two weeks is chronic suppurative otitis media, common in Uganda and with HIV.

options: chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (rest pain, ulcer or gangrene)

dx.pad.note: The ankle-brachial pressure index confirms it but is not in the test catalogue yet. Much foot ischaemia in Uganda is diabetic: examine feet and pulses at every diabetes visit.

dx.pancreatic_biliary_cancer.note: Painless progressive jaundice with pale stools, dark urine and itch is obstructive until ultrasound shows otherwise; a dilated biliary tree separates it from hepatitis. Fever is not used against it, because cholangitis complicates malignant strictures (especially after stenting).

dx.pancreatitis_acute.note: Needs two of: typical epigastric pain, lipase or amylase three times normal, imaging; alcohol and gallstones dominate, and triglycerides and calcium are the other causes to check. A perforated ulcer and an inferior MI are the mimics; the Revised Atlanta grading has no source id yet.

dx.paracetamol_overdose.must_not_miss_reason: Liver failure is preventable only if the antidote starts early, best within 8 hours of ingestion; patients look well until it is too late.
dx.paracetamol_overdose.note: Absent symptoms never argue against it in the first day; a timed paracetamol level and ALT decide, and treatment should not wait for a level that cannot be had within 8 hours. There is no field for time or amount of ingestion.

dx.parkinsonism.note: Drug-induced parkinsonism (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) must be excluded, but these medicines are not yet catalogue items. Early falls, early dementia or marked postural hypotension suggest an atypical parkinsonism.

dx.pcp.must_not_miss_reason: Hypoxic respiratory failure with high mortality in untreated advanced HIV; treatable, and adjunctive therapy depends on recognising hypoxia early.
dx.pcp.note: Dry cough and exertional breathlessness over weeks, with hypoxia out of proportion to a near-normal chest X-ray; desaturation on exertion is the bedside clue. Microbiological confirmation is rarely available, so seek TB in parallel; bacterial co-infection is common, so purulent sputum lowers the probability only modestly.

dx.peptic_ulcer.note: H. pylori and NSAIDs (including over-the-counter and herbal analgesics) are the drivers; an H. pylori test is not yet in the test catalogue. Weight loss, dysphagia, anaemia or a mass mean endoscopy to exclude gastric cancer.

dx.perforated_viscus.must_not_miss_reason: Generalised peritonitis and septic shock within hours; needs resuscitation, antibiotics and surgery.
dx.perforated_viscus.note: Perforated peptic ulcer and typhoid ileal perforation (second to third week of fever) are the leading causes in Uganda; an erect chest film shows free air in most. Older, immunosuppressed or steroid-treated patients may lack rigidity.

dx.pericardial_effusion.note: Most large effusions in Uganda are tuberculous, often with HIV; uraemia, malignancy and hypothyroidism are the others. Watch for tamponade: falling BP, rising JVP, pulsus paradoxus.

dx.pericarditis.note: Pain eased by sitting forward and worse lying flat is the key history, not yet captured by the chest pain question. TB (often with HIV) and uraemia are important causes here: echo every case for effusion.

dx.peripheral_neuropathy.note: Diabetes, HIV (and older ART such as stavudine), isoniazid without pyridoxine, alcohol and B12 deficiency are the common Ugandan causes. Weakness ascending over days is GBS until shown otherwise.

dx.pid.note: A pregnancy test is mandatory before this label because ectopic pregnancy is the dangerous mimic. Cervical motion and adnexal tenderness are not yet structured examination findings.

dx.pleural_effusion.note: TB is the leading cause of exudative effusion in Uganda, often with HIV; parapneumonic empyema, malignancy and heart, kidney or liver failure are the others. A diagnostic tap with Light's criteria separates exudate from transudate.

dx.pneumonia.note: In Uganda keep TB and, with HIV, PCP in the same differential; send Xpert when cough persists or HIV is present. CRB65 grades severity (NICE NG250), but SpO2 below 92% on air or advanced HIV is severe whatever the score.

dx.pneumothorax.must_not_miss_reason: Tension pneumothorax causes obstructive shock and arrest within minutes; it is a clinical diagnosis needing immediate decompression.
dx.pneumothorax.note: Secondary pneumothorax from TB, post-TB cavities, COPD and PCP is common in Uganda and worse tolerated than primary. Hypotension with tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds means tension: decompress before the X-ray.

dx.poisoning_medicine.must_not_miss_reason: Sedative, cardiotoxic and hypoglycaemic overdoses kill within hours, and paracetamol injury is silent until too late to prevent.
dx.poisoning_medicine.note: Send a paracetamol level in every intentional overdose whatever the stated drug, because co-ingestion is common and early paracetamol toxicity is silent. The medicine list records what is taken, not what or how much was swallowed; record that in free text.

dx.poisoning_nonmedicinal.must_not_miss_reason: Pesticide, paraffin, caustic and toxic-alcohol poisoning cause airway, respiratory and metabolic collapse within hours.
dx.poisoning_nonmedicinal.note: Pesticides (organophosphates, carbamates, rodenticides), paraffin, caustics and adulterated spirits dominate in Uganda, and self-poisoning is common, so ask about intent in private. Crackles after paraffin ingestion mean aspiration.

dx.poisoning_unknown.must_not_miss_reason: Many poisons in Uganda (pesticides, sedatives, toxic alcohols) cause respiratory failure, fits or arrhythmia within hours; supportive care and antidotes are time-dependent.
dx.poisoning_unknown.note: The history has no ingestion or exposure question, so substance, time, amount and intent are free text. Check glucose first in anyone with reduced consciousness; the toxidrome (secretions, fasciculations, slow breathing, acidotic breathing) points to the agent.

dx.post_tb_lung_disease.note: Its defining fact, previous TB, is a restricted (tb) history item and so is not offered as evidence on this standard diagnosis, which leaves the evidence non-specific (active TB, bronchiectasis, COPD and lung cancer fit equally): CSO to decide. Exclude active or relapsed TB (Xpert) before attributing symptoms to sequelae, and look for aspergilloma and cor pulmonale.

dx.pre_eclampsia.must_not_miss_reason: A leading cause of maternal death in Uganda; progression to severe disease and eclampsia is preventable when recognised.
dx.pre_eclampsia.note: Needs pregnancy beyond 20 weeks or the postpartum period, neither of which the history captures; proteinuria comes from the dipstick. Oedema alone is common in normal pregnancy.

dx.pre_eclampsia_severe.must_not_miss_reason: Imminent risk of eclampsia, stroke, HELLP, pulmonary oedema and abruption; seizure prevention and delivery planning cannot wait.
dx.pre_eclampsia_severe.note: BP atoms use the obstetric severe range (REF-DX-BP-OBST-SEVERE, 160/110), not the general 180/120 hypertensive-emergency threshold. Pregnancy status and gestation are not captured fields (a prerequisite before go-live), and MEOWS rather than NEWS2 applies in pregnancy (archive, oedema).

dx.pressure_injury.note: Record stage and site on the examination item; a stage 3 or 4 ulcer over bone with fever should prompt a search for osteomyelitis. Check the sacrum and heels of every bedbound patient on admission.

dx.prostate_cancer.note: Ugandan men often present with metastatic disease (bone pain, cord compression, anaemia), and Kampala incidence has roughly doubled since 1991 (archive, weight loss). Voiding symptoms alone do not separate it from benign enlargement, and a benign-feeling prostate does not exclude it.

dx.psychosis.note: First-episode psychosis needs an organic screen (HIV, syphilis, malaria, CNS infection, epilepsy, substances) before a primary label. Fever, disorientation or reduced consciousness point to delirium.

dx.pulmonary_embolism.must_not_miss_reason: Untreated PE has high early mortality and massive PE kills within hours; anticoagulation or thrombolysis is effective.
dx.pulmonary_embolism.note: Under-diagnosed in Uganda where CTPA and D-dimer are scarce: bedside echo (RV dilatation) and leg Doppler can decide in the unstable patient. Pregnancy, postpartum and oestrogen use have no history item yet; ask directly.

dx.pulmonary_hypertension.note: Ugandan causes: left-heart and rheumatic valve disease, post-TB and chronic lung disease, HIV, sickle cell disease, chronic PE and schistosomiasis (ask about fishing or lake exposure). Echo estimates the pressure (right-heart catheterisation is rarely available), and NYHA stands in for the WHO functional class.

dx.pyelonephritis.note: Infection behind an obstruction (stone, prostate, schistosomal stricture) needs urgent drainage: image with AKI or no response within 48 hours. Pregnancy, diabetes and male sex make it complicated.

dx.pyomyositis.note: Tropical pyomyositis (mostly S. aureus) is common in Uganda, often with HIV; the deep woody muscle swelling has no structured examination item. Ultrasound finds drainable pus, but the catalogue has no soft-tissue ultrasound test.

dx.rabies.note: Hydrophobia, aerophobia and fluctuating agitation weeks to months after an animal bite; the paralytic form mimics Guillain-Barre syndrome, and treatable encephalitis must be excluded before this label. Not must-not-miss because it is untreatable once symptomatic, but missing it leaves staff and family without prophylaxis: assess contacts; there is no history item for an animal bite.

dx.rabies_exposure.must_not_miss_reason: Clinical rabies is almost always fatal; timely wound care and post-exposure prophylaxis prevent it.
dx.rabies_exposure.note: The only structured atom (contact with sick or dead animals or bats, a fever red flag) misses most dog bites, so an animal bite or scratch history item is needed (CSO to request); until then this rests on the clinician's own record. The WHO exposure category and the animal's status decide prophylaxis; head, neck and hand bites and HIV make prompt action more important, and check tetanus status too.

dx.reduced_consciousness_unexplained.note: Check glucose first. In Uganda the common causes are cerebral malaria, meningitis (including cryptococcal and TB), stroke, sepsis, hypoglycaemia, organophosphate or other poisoning and metabolic encephalopathy.

dx.respiratory_failure.must_not_miss_reason: Unrecognised respiratory failure progresses to arrest; oxygen, ventilatory support and treatment of the cause are needed now.
dx.respiratory_failure.note: The type needs a blood gas; where hypercapnia is a risk get one early (BTS). A falling respiratory rate or new drowsiness in a tiring patient is pre-arrest, not improvement.

dx.rhabdomyolysis.note: Common triggers are a long lie after a fall or stroke, seizures, crush injury or assault, heat and exertion, snakebite, alcohol and statins. Dipstick positive for blood without red cells on microscopy suggests myoglobin.

dx.rheumatic_fever.note: Revised Jones criteria (2015) need evidence of recent streptococcal infection, and the ASO titre is not in the test catalogue yet. Uganda is a high-risk population, so subclinical carditis on echo counts as a major criterion.

dx.rheumatic_heart_disease.note: Uganda carries one of the highest RHD burdens: mitral disease presents in adolescents and young adults, often first as AF, stroke, haemoptysis or heart failure in pregnancy. Echo (WHF criteria) decides and grades valve severity, while NYHA grades symptoms only; there is no past-history item for rheumatic fever yet.

dx.rheumatoid_arthritis.note: Symmetrical small-joint synovitis with morning stiffness over an hour. Chikungunya, HIV-associated arthritis and SLE mimic it in Uganda; chikungunya is not yet a catalogue term.

dx.rickettsial.note: Look for an eschar (no specific item: record it as a skin ulcer) with regional nodes after tick exposure; louse-borne typhus occurs in crowded settings. No rickettsial test is in the catalogue, so response to empirical treatment is often the practical confirmation.

dx.sah.must_not_miss_reason: Early rebleeding is often fatal; a warning bleed with a thunderclap headache is the chance to find and secure the aneurysm.
dx.sah.note: CT is most sensitive within 6 hours of onset; a normal CT after that needs LP for xanthochromia at least 12 hours after onset. Neck stiffness takes hours to develop, so its absence does not exclude SAH.

dx.sbp.must_not_miss_reason: Often silent, and untreated SBP precipitates kidney failure, encephalopathy and death within days.
dx.sbp.note: Fever and pain are often absent: tap every admitted patient with ascites, and any with new encephalopathy, AKI or GI bleeding (ascitic neutrophils 250/mm3 or more); ultrasound-only ascites counts, so clinical absence of ascites does not exclude it. A lymphocytic ascites with high protein points to TB peritonitis, common in Uganda.

dx.scabies.note: Night itch and itching household contacts are the clues and are not structured items. Crusted scabies suggests immunosuppression and is highly contagious.

dx.schistosomiasis.note: S. mansoni around Lakes Victoria and Albert causes periportal fibrosis with preserved liver function: massive splenomegaly and variceal bleeding in a young adult without jaundice. Freshwater contact (fishing, bathing, washing) is the key history; jaundice points to a second cause.

dx.seizure_unexplained.note: A first adult seizure in Uganda needs glucose, malaria testing, HIV testing (toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal and TB disease) and a pregnancy check for eclampsia; alcohol withdrawal and neurocysticercosis are common. Brief jerks during a faint (convulsive syncope) are not a seizure.

dx.sepsis.must_not_miss_reason: Mortality rises with every hour of delayed antimicrobials and fluids.
dx.sepsis.note: No qSOFA (SSC 2026 prefers NEWS2 for screening); septic shock is its own term, not a grade of this one. Look for the source (chest, urine, abdomen, skin and pressure areas, CNS, lines, catheters and wounds); malaria is the first test in Uganda.

dx.septic_arthritis.must_not_miss_reason: Destroys the joint within days and can cause sepsis; aspirate before antibiotics.
dx.septic_arthritis.note: Aspirate any hot swollen joint: crystals do not exclude infection. In young sexually active adults consider disseminated gonococcal infection, and in sickle cell disease Salmonella.

dx.septic_shock.must_not_miss_reason: Refractory hypotension with hypoperfusion; mortality is high and time-dependent.
dx.septic_shock.note: Sepsis-3 requires vasopressors for MAP 65 and lactate over 2 despite fluids; at the bedside hypotension with hypoperfusion is the working label. Exclude haemorrhage, cardiogenic shock and, in Uganda, severe malaria.

dx.shock_unexplained.note: Sort by skin and JVP: warm with a low JVP is distributive, cold with a low JVP hypovolaemic, cold with a high JVP cardiogenic or obstructive (tamponade, tension pneumothorax, PE). Bedside ultrasound answers most of this in minutes.

dx.sickle_cell_crisis.must_not_miss_reason: Acute chest syndrome, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis and stroke kill within hours to days and need specific treatment beyond analgesia.
dx.sickle_cell_crisis.note: New chest signs, hypoxia or fever during a pain crisis are acute chest syndrome until proven otherwise; a falling haemoglobin with a growing spleen is sequestration, and a low reticulocyte count points to aplastic crisis. Malaria and bacterial infection are the common precipitants in Uganda, and abdominal crises mimic a surgical abdomen.

dx.sickle_cell_disease.note: Some Ugandan adults reach the ward undiagnosed or with an unconfirmed label; confirm with haemoglobin electrophoresis, since a sickling test does not separate disease from trait. Splenomegaly persists into adulthood in a minority of Ugandan HbSS patients (malaria exposure; HbC is essentially absent here), so a spleen does not exclude sickle cell disease.

dx.sjs_ten.must_not_miss_reason: Mortality is high and rises with delay in withdrawing the culprit drug; eye and mucosal involvement scars permanently.
dx.sjs_ten.note: Co-trimoxazole, nevirapine, anti-TB drugs and anticonvulsants are the usual culprits in Uganda, and HIV raises the risk many-fold. The history records medicines taken, not start dates; ask when each began (4 to 28 days before is typical).

dx.skin_abscess.note: Recurrent abscesses warrant a glucose and an HIV test. Deep woody swelling in a large muscle without surface pus suggests pyomyositis, common in the tropics.

dx.sle.note: Mostly women of reproductive age; lupus nephritis is silent until late, so check urine and BP in every suspected case. HIV, TB and drug reactions mimic its rash, cytopenias and serositis.

dx.snakebite.must_not_miss_reason: Coagulopathy, neurotoxic paralysis and AKI can develop over hours after a quiet start; antivenom works best early.
dx.snakebite.note: The history has no bite question and the examination no bite-site item; unilateral limb swelling and blistering are the proxies. Repeat the 20-minute clotting test and neurological checks, since coagulopathy and ptosis can appear hours after a normal first assessment.

dx.space_occupying_lesion.must_not_miss_reason: Raised intracranial pressure can cause herniation, and the commonest lesions in advanced HIV (toxoplasmosis, tuberculoma) are treatable.
dx.space_occupying_lesion.note: In advanced HIV think toxoplasmosis, tuberculoma, primary CNS lymphoma and cryptococcoma; otherwise metastases, primary tumours and neurocysticercosis in pig-keeping areas. Image before LP when papilloedema or focal signs suggest a mass.

dx.splenomegaly_unexplained.note: Massive spleens in Uganda: hyper-reactive malarial splenomegaly, chronic myeloid leukaemia, visceral leishmaniasis (north-east), schistosomal portal hypertension and lymphoma. Record size in centimetres below the costal margin to follow change.
